title: Truly canonical books were never so doubtful
source_text: XXXV. Ad secundam vero illam probationem petitam ex libris de quibus olim dubitatum est, quasi librorum quorundam divinorum fuerit olim dubia authoritas, quoniam Ecclesia super illis sententiam suam nondum pronunciarat: postea vero omnis dubitatio sublata fuerit per Ecclesiae judicium & definitionem: Dico primo librorum qui vere divini & Canonici sunt authoritatem nunquam ita fuisse dubiam, ut de iis aliquando dubitare licuerit, amplius vero non liceat, quod Pontificii volunt. Etenim qui dubitarunt de Epistola ad Hebraeos, & Joannis Apocalypsi, aliisque Novi Testamenti libris, id temere fecerunt, & sine justa ratione. Et sicut hodie culpa non careret qui librorum illorum authoritatem negaret, aut in dubium vocaret, ita quoque fuerunt reprehensione digni, qui libris istis olim authoritatem sustulerunt, aut dubios eos reddere voluerunt. Quod attinet autem caeteros illos libros, quos ad Veteris Testamenti Canonem Pontificii pertinere volunt, & de quibus tamen agnoscunt licuisse olim dubitare, quemadmodum merito de illis dubitatum fuit, ita quoque hodie jure dubitari posse contendimus.
pass_a_gloss: But to that second proof drawn from the books about which there was once doubt, as if the authority of certain divine books was once doubtful because the Church had not yet pronounced her sentence upon them, and afterward all doubt was removed by the Church's judgment and definition: I say first that the authority of books which are truly divine and Canonical never was so doubtful that it was once lawful to doubt concerning them and afterward is no longer lawful, which is what the Pontificians want. For those who doubted concerning the Epistle to the Hebrews, and John's Apocalypse, and other books of the New Testament, did that rashly and without just reason. And just as today he would not be without blame who should deny the authority of those books or call it into doubt, so also those were worthy of censure who once took authority away from those books or wished to render them doubtful. But as for those other books which the Pontificians want to belong to the Canon of the Old Testament, and about which they nevertheless acknowledge it was once lawful to doubt: just as they were rightly doubted then, so also we contend that today they can rightly be doubted.
pass_b_english: Next, their second proof from books once doubted — as if certain divine books were once of doubtful authority because the Church had not yet spoken, and all doubt later fell by the Church's judgment and definition.
I say first: the authority of books that are truly divine and canonical was never so doubtful that it was once lawful to doubt them and later unlawful, which is what the Pontificians claim.

Those who doubted Hebrews, John's Apocalypse, and other New Testament books did so rashly and without just cause. Just as today anyone who denied or questioned those books' authority would not be blameless, so those who once stripped them of authority or tried to make them doubtful deserved blame.

But as for the other books Rome wants in the Old Testament Canon, about which they themselves grant it was once lawful to doubt: as they were rightly doubted then, so we contend they may rightly be doubted still.
